name: Propranolol (Inderal LA, Inderal XL, InnoPran XL, Hemangeol)
summary: Nonselective beta-blocker used in psychiatry mainly for the body symptoms of anxiety (performance anxiety), antipsychotic-induced akathisia, and medication-related tremor. Works in about 30–60 minutes for situational use, but it can lower heart rate and trigger bronchospasm in people with asthma.
description: Propranolol doesn’t “erase” anxiety thoughts — it turns down the adrenaline surge (shaky hands, pounding heart, sweating, voice tremor). That makes it a go-to for performance anxiety and sometimes for antipsychotic-induced akathisia or lithium tremor. Biggest risks are low heart rate, low blood pressure, dizziness, fatigue, and breathing trouble in people with asthma/COPD. Don’t stop it abruptly if you’ve been taking it daily.
patient_summary: Propranolol is for the physical side of anxiety — not the mental spiral. If your issue is shaky hands, racing heart, or visible nerves before a talk, it can be a game-changer. If your issue is constant worry all day, it’s usually not the right tool by itself. The tradeoff: it can make you feel tired, lightheaded, or “slower,” and it’s a no-go for many people with asthma.

linked_conditions.context: Best fit when anxiety shows up as a strong body response (tremor, palpitations, sweating) right before a specific event. Not a primary treatment for ongoing generalized anxiety.
Often used when antipsychotics cause restlessness and an inability to sit still. Typically used as a symptom-targeting add-on while the main medication plan is adjusted.
Can reduce tremor from psychiatric meds (especially lithium) when dose reduction or switching isn’t possible or would destabilize mood.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to propranolol, beta-blockers, or any component of the formulation
Uncompensated heart failure (except select tachyarrhythmia-related scenarios under specialist care)
Second- or third-degree heart block (unless a functioning pacemaker is present)

efficacy_response.metric: Reduction of physical anxiety symptoms during a performance situation
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Depends on dose, timing, and baseline heart rate; not a one-size-fits-all response
efficacy_response.patient_text: For performance anxiety, propranolol tends to help the visible and uncomfortable “adrenaline” symptoms (shaking, pounding heart, voice tremor). It usually doesn’t fix anxious thoughts by itself — it just makes your body stop yelling so your brain can do the job.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: General clinical use; evidence quality varies by indication

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid and complete (oral), with significant first-pass metabolism
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: ~25% (variable; can increase with food and higher-protein diets)
pharmacokinetics.onset: Oral beta-blockade: ~1 to 2 hours; IV: ≤5 minutes
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate-release: ~1 to 4 hours; some extended-release products peak later
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Immediate-release: ~3 to 6 hours; extended-release: ~8 to 10 hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism (CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 major pathways; CYP2C19 minor; CYP3A4 minor); active metabolite 4-hydroxypropranolol has beta-blocking activity
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: IR tablets are typically taken on an empty stomach; food can increase serum levels. ER capsules may be taken with or without food but should be consistent.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: In psychiatry, propranolol is mostly a “body symptoms” medication. It doesn’t directly treat the core thoughts of anxiety — it dampens the adrenaline response so your hands stop shaking and your heart stops trying to escape your chest.
items: Performance anxiety (off-label): Situational anxiety with prominent physical symptoms (tremor, palpitations, sweating, voice shakiness)
Antipsychotic-induced akathisia (off-label): Restlessness, pacing, can’t-sit-still feeling after starting or increasing an antipsychotic
Medication-induced tremor (off-label): Tremor related to psychiatric meds, especially lithium
off_label: Situational tremor control when symptoms spike during specific events
Adrenergic symptom control during medication side effect episodes when clinically appropriate

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s different, but this is the usual “feel” of propranolol when it’s working — and when it’s not.

quotes: My hands stopped shaking, which was the whole point.
My heart didn’t race, so I could actually focus on what I was saying.
I still felt nervous, but I didn’t look nervous.
That inner motor calmed down enough that I could sit still.
The pacing urge eased — not perfect, but way more tolerable.
It didn’t fix everything, but it took the edge off.
items.note: Akathisia can be dangerous and miserable. If it’s severe, the main plan usually involves adjusting the antipsychotic and adding targeted treatment — propranolol may be one piece of that.

quotes: I felt a little flat and tired for a few hours.
Standing up fast made me a bit dizzy.
It helped the shakes, but I felt slower.

items.category: Sleep and dreams can get weird
quotes: I had vivid dreams I don’t usually get.
My sleep felt lighter, like I wasn’t fully resting.
Nightmares popped up when I started it.
items.note: Propranolol is lipophilic and can affect the central nervous system in some people (fatigue, insomnia, vivid dreams).

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: For psychiatry uses, timing matters. Propranolol is usually chosen because you can predict when you’ll need it (like a presentation) or because you want steady symptom control (like akathisia or medication tremor).
key_points: 30–60 minutes: Many people notice performance-anxiety benefit in this window (especially physical symptoms)
1–2 hours: Oral beta-blockade effect is typically established; this is often when the “steady” effect feels most noticeable
6–12 hours: Typical effect window for immediate-release tablets
~24 hours: Extended-release forms can provide all-day coverage (not usually necessary for performance-only use)
IV onset is minutes, but IV use is a medical setting workflow — not a psychiatry outpatient anxiety strategy

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Propranolol is usually most effective when the problem is the adrenaline surge — tremor, pounding heart, sweating, shaky voice — especially in performance situations. If the main issue is nonstop worry, rumination, dread, or panic spirals, propranolol tends to be less satisfying as a standalone treatment.
sections.clinical_details: For performance anxiety, clinicians commonly use immediate-release dosing ahead of an event, with a trial run beforehand to check tolerability (blood pressure, dizziness, fatigue). For akathisia and medication-induced tremor, dosing is typically scheduled (not just PRN) and adjusted gradually based on response and heart rate/blood pressure tolerance.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This medication can slow your heart rate and lower blood pressure. If you have asthma or significant breathing issues, it can trigger bronchospasm.
other: Do not use if you have bronchial asthma; nonselective beta-blockers can cause bronchospasm and breathing emergencies
Can cause bradycardia (slow heart rate), hypotension (low blood pressure), dizziness, fainting, and worsening conduction problems (heart block)
May worsen or unmask heart failure in susceptible patients; requires careful monitoring if there is underlying cardiac disease
Can mask warning signs of hypoglycemia (like tremor and palpitations); sweating may be the only obvious symptom
May cause fatigue, sleep disruption, vivid dreams, and (less commonly) mood changes
Do not stop abruptly if taken daily — sudden withdrawal can cause rebound tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, and (in high-risk patients) chest pain or arrhythmias
patient_counseling: If you’re using this for performance anxiety: do a trial dose on a normal day first — you don’t want your first test run to be on stage.
If you feel wheezing, chest tightness, or new breathing trouble, stop and get urgent medical help — especially if you have asthma history.
Stand up slowly if you’re prone to dizziness. Hydrate. Don’t mix with other meds that also lower heart rate unless your clinician is actively managing that combination.
If you have diabetes or you’re prone to low blood sugar, be extra cautious — propranolol can hide your usual warning signs.
If you’ve been taking it daily, taper — don’t quit suddenly.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common issues are fatigue, dizziness/lightheadedness, cold hands/feet, sleep changes (insomnia or vivid dreams), and slower heart rate. Side effects are more likely if your baseline blood pressure or heart rate runs low.
plain_language_list: Dizziness, especially when standing up fast
Sexual side effects (can happen, but not everyone)

common.patient_note: Some people feel a “weighted blanket” body sensation — calmer, but also less pep. This is one reason performance dosing is often kept low and tested in advance.
Usually related to blood pressure lowering. If you’re feeling faint or getting tunnel vision when you stand, the dose may be too high or you may not be a good match for this medication.
Propranolol can affect sleep quality in some people. If dreams get intense or insomnia ramps up, dose timing changes or switching strategies may help.
If your heart rate drops too low (or you feel weak, faint, or short of breath), this needs medical attention and dose adjustment.

serious: Bronchospasm (especially in asthma/COPD): wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness. MEDICAL EMERGENCY if severe.
Severe bradycardia, heart block, or fainting episodes: urgent evaluation needed.
Worsening heart failure symptoms: swelling, shortness of breath, rapid weight gain, fatigue out of proportion.
Severe hypoglycemia risk and masked warning signs (especially in infants/children, and in adults with diabetes on glucose-lowering therapy).
Withdrawal reactions after abrupt stoppage in chronic users: rebound tachycardia, hypertension, chest pain, arrhythmias.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Most dangerous interactions are the ones that stack heart-rate-lowering effects or worsen breathing/glucose risk.

items.with: Other AV node / heart-rate lowering meds (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, ivabradine; some antiarrhythmics)
items.risk: Excessive bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, fainting.
items.action: Use only with clinician oversight. Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, and symptoms closely, especially after dose changes.

items.risk: Propranolol can blunt the effect of rescue inhalers and may worsen bronchospasm.
items.action: Avoid if you have asthma. If you have COPD or reactive airway symptoms, discuss safer alternatives (often a beta-1 selective blocker if a beta-blocker is needed at all).

items.with: Diabetes medications (insulin, sulfonylureas and others that can cause hypoglycemia)
items.risk: Propranolol can prolong hypoglycemia and hide warning signs like tremor and palpitations.
items.action: Monitor glucose carefully, especially during dose changes or illness/poor intake. Educate that sweating may be the main visible warning sign.

items.risk: Alcohol can unpredictably raise or lower propranolol levels and can worsen dizziness and blood pressure drops.
items.action: Use caution. If you’re using propranolol for performance, avoid experimenting with alcohol the same day.

items.risk: Cigarette smoking can lower propranolol levels and reduce effect in some people.
items.action: If you change smoking status (start/stop), your dose response may change too.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been taking propranolol daily (akathisia or tremor schedules), don’t stop abruptly. A gradual taper helps prevent rebound symptoms like fast heart rate and blood pressure spikes. If you only use it rarely (performance PRN), tapering usually isn’t necessary.
key_points: Daily use: taper down over at least several days to 2 weeks, depending on dose, duration, and cardiac risk profile.
Higher-risk patients (heart disease, angina history): taper more cautiously and involve cardiology if needed.
Rebound can show up within 24–48 hours after abrupt stopping in chronic users (fast heart rate, elevated BP, shakiness).
If propranolol was being used for akathisia, plan for symptom monitoring during taper and make sure the antipsychotic side effect plan is addressed (dose change, switch, or additional targeted meds).

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Psychiatry dosing is usually immediate-release (IR), because you either want predictable timing (performance anxiety) or flexible titration (akathisia, tremor). Extended-release is more of a “steady all-day” option and is not typically necessary for performance-only use.

adult.performance_anxiety_prn: 10 to 20 mg PO once, taken 30 to 60 minutes before the anxiety-provoking situation; if not enough, increase by 10 to 20 mg before a future situation; maximum 60 mg per event
adult.akathisia_titration: If needed, adjust based on response and tolerability at intervals of ≥1 week
adult.lithium_tremor_titration: Titrate based on response and tolerability; aim for the lowest effective dose that reduces tremor while keeping heart rate and blood pressure safe

sections.simple_explanation: For performance anxiety, propranolol is usually a low-dose one-time pill before an event. For akathisia or medication tremor, it’s usually scheduled dosing and adjusted gradually. The goal is symptom relief without making your heart rate or blood pressure drop too much.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Propranolol can be used in pregnancy when clinically necessary, but it’s not usually the first-choice beta-blocker for pregnancy hypertension. Late-pregnancy exposure can affect newborn heart rate and glucose. In breastfeeding, it’s generally considered compatible at usual doses, but infants should be monitored.
sections.pregnancy: Crosses the placenta. Third-trimester exposure may increase risk of neonatal bradycardia, hypoglycemia, hypotension, and respiratory depression. If used during pregnancy, clinicians typically monitor fetal growth and monitor the newborn for at least 48 hours after delivery for bradycardia, hypoglycemia, and respiratory effects. For psychiatric performance anxiety, clinicians often try non-med options first in pregnancy unless symptoms are significantly impairing and benefits outweigh risks.
sections.lactation: Propranolol and inactive metabolites appear in breast milk. At usual doses it is often considered compatible with breastfeeding, but monitor the infant for bradycardia, cyanosis, and hypoglycemia, especially in very young infants or if maternal doses are higher.
sections.geriatrics: Use caution and consider lower starting doses. Older adults are more prone to bradycardia, hypotension, dizziness, and falls. If used, titrate slowly and monitor closely, especially with other heart-rate-lowering medications.
sections.hepatic: Use caution in hepatic impairment; accumulation can be significant with cirrhosis. For many non-variceal indications, immediate-release is preferred for flexible titration. In moderate to severe cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C), a common approach is ≤50% of the usual indication-specific dose no more frequently than twice daily, with slower adjustments (every 3 to 5 days or longer) based on response and tolerability.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment is generally required for kidney impairment or dialysis, but use caution during initiation in advanced kidney disease because patients may be more prone to side effects.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Heart rate and blood pressure: baseline and after dose changes; watch for symptomatic bradycardia or hypotension (dizziness, fainting).
Respiratory symptoms: wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness — especially in anyone with asthma/COPD history.
Mental alertness and fatigue: sedation-like tiredness can show up, especially early or at higher doses.
Sleep effects: insomnia, vivid dreams, nightmares — track whether timing changes help.
Akathisia tracking (if relevant): symptom rating over time (restlessness, pacing, inner agitation) and safety monitoring for severe distress.
Tremor tracking (if relevant): functional impact (writing, eating, phone use) and whether benefit is worth side effects.
Blood glucose awareness in diabetes: propranolol can mask hypoglycemia symptoms; educate on sweating as a key warning sign.
Medication review for interactions: especially other heart-rate-lowering agents and any regimen changes.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Psychiatry use usually relies on immediate-release tablets because dosing is low and timing matters. Extended-release can be useful when symptoms need steady all-day control, but it’s less common for performance-only use.
items: Immediate-release tablets (generic): 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, 60 mg, 80 mg
Extended-release capsules (generic and brand): 60 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg, 160 mg (Inderal LA, Inderal XL, InnoPran XL; strengths vary by product)
Oral solution (generic): 20 mg/5 mL (4 mg/mL) and 40 mg/5 mL (8 mg/mL)
Oral solution (Hemangeol): 4.28 mg/mL (primarily for infantile hemangioma use)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Propranolol is a nonselective beta-blocker. It blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, which lowers heart rate and reduces the physical effects of adrenaline. In psychiatry, that translates to fewer outward anxiety symptoms like tremor, palpitations, and shaky voice — the “fight-or-flight” part gets quieter.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Propranolol is a symptom-targeting tool. For performance anxiety, it’s often used PRN when physical symptoms are the main problem and you need predictable timing. For akathisia, it’s typically used as part of a broader plan that also addresses the causative antipsychotic (dose reduction, switch, or additional treatments). For medication-induced tremor (like lithium tremor), it can reduce tremor without destabilizing mood when changing the primary medication isn’t feasible.

seo.title: Propranolol (Inderal): Performance Anxiety, Akathisia, Tremor — Uses, Dosing, Side Effects
seo.description: Propranolol for psychiatry uses: performance anxiety (PRN 10–20 mg), antipsychotic-induced akathisia, and medication tremor. Onset, dosing, side effects (fatigue, dizziness, low heart rate), and key safety warnings (asthma, bradycardia, tapering).

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: It treats the physical side of anxiety — the adrenaline symptoms. Think: shaky hands, pounding heart, sweating, voice tremor. It usually doesn’t remove anxious thoughts the way therapy, SSRIs, or other anxiety treatments can.

faqs.q: How do I take propranolol for performance anxiety?
faqs.a: Typical approach is immediate-release 10–20 mg taken 30–60 minutes before the event. If that’s not enough and you tolerate it well, some people increase in 10–20 mg steps on future events, up to 60 mg per event. Always do a trial run on a normal day first.

faqs.q: Will propranolol make me feel sleepy or weird?
faqs.a: It can. The most common “weird” feelings are fatigue, low energy, lightheadedness, and sometimes vivid dreams or sleep disruption. If you feel faint, your dose may be too high — or you may not be a good match for this med.

faqs.q: Can propranolol help akathisia from antipsychotics?
faqs.a: Yes, sometimes. Propranolol is commonly used as an add-on for antipsychotic-induced akathisia. But akathisia often needs a bigger plan too — adjusting the antipsychotic (dose change or switch) is usually part of the solution.
It can reduce lithium-related tremor in many people. Dosing is usually scheduled (not PRN), and the goal is the lowest dose that helps tremor without dropping heart rate or blood pressure too much.

People with bronchial asthma generally should not take propranolol because it can trigger bronchospasm. It’s also not appropriate for certain heart rhythm/conduction problems (like significant heart block), severe bradycardia, cardiogenic shock, or uncompensated heart failure unless a specialist is directing care.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol if I’m taking propranolol?
faqs.a: Use caution. Alcohol can worsen dizziness and blood pressure drops, and it can make propranolol’s effects less predictable. If you’re using propranolol for a performance event, don’t experiment with alcohol that same day.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper propranolol?
faqs.a: If you take it daily, yes — don’t stop abruptly. Tapering helps avoid rebound fast heart rate and blood pressure spikes. If you use it rarely and only PRN for performance anxiety, tapering usually isn’t needed.

Immediate-release tablets often last about 6–12 hours. Extended-release forms can cover about a full day. For performance anxiety, many people only need the immediate-release effect window around the event.
